## Overview

`ssGSEA3.0` runs single-sample Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (ssGSEA) on gene-centric
expression data, and PTM-Signature Enrichment Analysis (PTM-SEA) on site-centric
phosphoproteomics data scored against the directional
[PTM signatures database (PTMsigDB)](https://proteogenomics.shinyapps.io/ptmsigdb/).
Significance is assessed by feature-level (gene- or site-level) bootstrap
resampling, replacing the gene-label permutation testing used by `ssGSEA2.0`.

This vignette reproduces the biological comparisons from the ssGSEA3.0
manuscript (Clark and Mani), using the same three implementations throughout:

- **ssGSEA2.0-orig** -- `ssGSEA2.0` as published (Krug et al. 2019);
- **ssGSEA2.0-fixed** -- `ssGSEA2.0` with its correlation-vector reordering
  fixed, available on the
  [`ssGSEA2.0-fixed` branch](https://github.com/broadinstitute/ssGSEA3.0/tree/ssGSEA2.0-fixed)
  of this repository and archived at
  [doi:10.5281/zenodo.23734330](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23734330);
- **ssGSEA3.0** -- this package, archived at
  [doi:10.5281/zenodo.23734262](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23734262).

It covers:

1. *why* the bootstrap replaced permutation,
2. ssGSEA on lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) NMF factors against the MSigDB HALLMARK
   collection (manuscript Supplementary Figure 1),
3. the same factors against the larger, more diverse REACTOME collection
   (manuscript Figure 2), and
4. directional PTM-SEA on a PI3Kα-inhibitor phosphoproteomics dataset
   (manuscript Figure 3).

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(ssGSEA3)
```

### About the bundled results

The results loaded below, bundled with this package in `inst/extdata/`, are the
exact outputs reported in the manuscript and its Supplementary Tables 1-3.
If you run the `ssGSEA3()` calls shown below with the current package, your
numbers will differ slightly from these, and **the differences are due to
bootstrap randomness alone**. The scoring and significance algorithm is the same.

The manuscript's ssGSEA3.0 runs were made before commit `7303e16`. Before that
commit, `par = TRUE` gave each parallel worker its own random-number stream,
and which gene sets a worker scored depended on timing, so a seed did not fix
which random draws each gene set's bootstrap used. The current package gives
every gene set its own stream, so `seed = 42` now reproduces the same results
on every run. Those results are a different random draw from the manuscript's,
so counts near the significance threshold shift slightly (for example, 805
rather than 808 significant REACTOME gene sets at `weight = 1`), and the
conclusions are unchanged. `ssGSEA2.0` has no seed parameter, so its results
also vary slightly from run to run for the same reason.

## Why bootstrap instead of permutation?

### Weighted scoring under permutation is miscalibrated

ssGSEA computes a running-sum enrichment score in which each feature's
contribution is scaled by a `weight` parameter: `weight = 0` is a rank-only
score, and `weight > 0` favors features with larger expression magnitude.
`ssGSEA2.0-orig` assesses significance by permuting gene labels, and in doing so
reorders each feature's weight (the "correlation vector") together with its
rank. For `weight > 0` this makes highly expressed features drive the permuted
scores, giving a null distribution that is too narrow and inflating false
positives (GitHub issue #45 against `ssGSEA2.0`).

Scoring 400 randomly constructed (null) gene sets against the LUAD data shows
this directly. At `weight = 0.75`, `ssGSEA2.0-orig` calls 11.6% of null gene
sets significant at p < 0.05, against an expected 5%. Holding the weight vector
fixed in its observed order and permuting only gene-set membership
(`ssGSEA2.0-fixed`) brings this back to 5.2%. `ssGSEA3.0` gives 6.25%, and its
null p-values are the only ones at `weight = 0.75` not significantly different
from uniform (Kolmogorov-Smirnov p = 0.44).

### The fix costs detection power; the bootstrap recovers it

`ssGSEA2.0-fixed` restores calibration, but finds noticeably fewer significant
pathways at nonzero weight -- including biologically relevant ones (see the
REACTOME example below). In a synthetic simulation with a known embedded ±0.5
shift (10,000 gene sets of 20 members, `weight = 1`), `ssGSEA3.0` detected
significantly more true positives than `ssGSEA2.0-fixed` (4,629 vs. 4,211;
odds ratio 3.11, McNemar p < 0.0001). `ssGSEA3.0` replaces gene-label permutation with
bootstrap resampling of the measured features themselves, sampled with
replacement. Each bootstrap draw is re-ranked by its resampled values and the
gene set's members are relocated within that ranking, while each feature's
weight is always taken from the original data in its original order. The
bootstrap scores are centered to their own mean, their standard deviation is
used as a bootstrap standard error, and the p-value comes from the resulting
z-score. NES is the observed score divided by the mean of the same-signed
centered bootstrap scores.

### Directional (PTM-SEA) scoring

PTM-SEA's directional gene sets (`;u`/`;d`-labeled "up" and "down" members) are
scored by combining separately computed up and down sub-scores; with
`ssGSEA3.0` both are rescored from the same bootstrap draw. In a synthetic
simulation with a known embedded ±0.5 shift (10,000 gene sets of 20 members,
`weight = 0`), both permutation and bootstrap were well-calibrated under the
null, and the bootstrap found significantly more true positives for both
non-directional (428 bootstrap-only vs. 229 permutation-only; odds ratio 1.87,
McNemar p < 0.0001) and directional gene sets (390 vs. 296; odds ratio 1.32,
McNemar p = 0.0004). On real data the gain is much larger for directional
scoring, as Example 3 shows.

## Helpers used below

All three examples count a gene set as significant if it passes the FDR
threshold in at least one sample (not by counting gene-set x sample cells,
which would double-count gene sets significant in several samples), and draw
side-by-side heatmaps with one shared row order and color scale so the panels
can be compared directly:

```{r helpers}
## gene sets significant (FDR < fdr.max) in >= 1 sample
is_sig <- function(res, fdr.max) apply(res$fdr < fdr.max, 1, any)

## pooled NES correlation across all gene sets and samples
nes_cor <- function(a, b, method = "pearson") {
  cor(as.vector(a$scores), as.vector(b$scores), method = method)
}

## one plot_ssgsea_heatmap() panel per implementation, sharing the first
## panel's row clustering and one color scale (1st/99th percentile clamp of
## the plotted NES across all panels). `labels` optionally shortens long
## gene set names for display.
compare_heatmaps <- function(results, terms, fdr.max, labels = NULL) {
  if (!is.null(labels)) {
    new <- setNames(labels(terms), terms)
    results <- lapply(results, function(r) {
      r <- r[c("scores", "fdr", "sample.names", "output.score.type")]
      r$scores <- r$scores[terms, , drop = FALSE]
      r$fdr <- r$fdr[terms, , drop = FALSE]
      rownames(r$scores) <- rownames(r$fdr) <- r$gs.names <- unname(new[terms])
      r
    })
    terms <- unname(new[terms])
  }
  nes <- unlist(lapply(results, function(r) r$scores[terms, ]))
  q <- quantile(nes, c(0.01, 0.99))
  nes.range <- c(floor(q[1]), ceiling(q[2]))
  first <- results[[1]]$scores
  shared.clustering <- function(m) hclust(dist(first[rownames(m), , drop = FALSE]))
  n <- length(results)
  panels <- lapply(seq_len(n), function(i) {
    ht <- plot_ssgsea_heatmap(results[[i]], terms = terms, fdr.max = fdr.max,
                              cluster_rows = shared.clustering, nes.range = nes.range,
                              title = names(results)[i], title_fontsize = 10,
                              show_category = i == 1, show_row_dend = i == 1,
                              show_row_names = i == n, show_heatmap_legend = i == n)
    ## concatenated heatmaps need unique names; only the last panel's ("NES")
    ## is ever shown, as its legend title
    if (i < n) ht@name <- paste0("NES_", i)
    ## angled, so titles wider than their narrow panels don't collide
    ht@column_title_param$rot <- 45
    ht@column_title_param$just <- c(0, 0.5)
    ht
  })
  ComplexHeatmap::draw(Reduce(`+`, panels), ht_gap = grid::unit(6, "mm"))
}

## REACTOME names run past 70 characters: drop the prefix and underscores,
## and cut long names at a word boundary
short_reactome <- function(x, max.chars = 42) {
  x <- gsub("_", " ", sub("^REACTOME_", "", x))
  cut <- sub("\\s+\\S*$", "", substr(x, 1, max.chars))
  ifelse(nchar(x) > max.chars, paste0(cut, "..."), x)
}

method.names <- c(orig = "ssGSEA2.0-orig", fixed = "ssGSEA2.0-fixed", v3 = "ssGSEA3.0")
```

## Example 1: ssGSEA on LUAD NMF factors, HALLMARK

The bundled LUAD dataset holds the feature weights from non-negative matrix
factorization (NMF) of a lung adenocarcinoma cohort (Satpathy et al. 2025),
derived with the PANOPLY pipeline. Its four factors are named after their
published biological identities: Unstable-proliferative, Quiescent-EGFR,
Immune-active-KRAS and Stable-early-stage. The original publication scored
these against MSigDB HALLMARK v6.2 at `weight = 1` and FDR < 0.01:

```{r luad-score, eval = FALSE}
res <- ssGSEA3(
  input.ds = system.file("example", "LUAD_matrix_W_combined_signed_gc.gct", package = "ssGSEA3"),
  output.prefix = "luad",
  gene.set.databases = system.file("example", "h.all.v6.2.symbols.gmt", package = "ssGSEA3"),
  sample.norm.type = "rank", weight = 1, correl.type = "z.score",
  statistic = "area.under.RES", min.overlap = 10, nperm = 1000, seed = 42
)
```

This takes about 0.8 minutes on 10 cores (`ssGSEA2.0-orig`: about 0.5 minutes).
Here we load the manuscript's results for all three implementations, at both
`weight = 1` and `weight = 0`:

```{r luad-load}
luad <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "luad_hallmark_manuscript_results.rds",
                            package = "ssGSEA3"))
luad$weight1$v3
fdr.hallmark <- 0.01

sig.hallmark <- sapply(c("weight0", "weight1"), function(w) {
  sapply(luad[[w]], function(r) sum(is_sig(r, fdr.hallmark)))
})
dimnames(sig.hallmark) <- list(method.names, c("weight = 0", "weight = 1"))
sig.hallmark
```

```{r luad-compare, include = FALSE}
s1 <- lapply(luad$weight1, is_sig, fdr.max = fdr.hallmark)
```

At `weight = 0`, where the correlation-vector reordering cannot occur, all three
implementations find `r sig.hallmark[1, 1]` significant gene sets. At
`weight = 1`, fixing the reordering drops `ssGSEA2.0-orig`'s
`r sig.hallmark[1, 2]` to `r sig.hallmark[2, 2]`, while `ssGSEA3.0` finds
`r sig.hallmark[3, 2]`, keeping `r sum(s1$orig & s1$v3 & !s1$fixed)` that
`ssGSEA2.0-fixed` lost. The results nonetheless agree closely:
`r sum(s1$fixed & s1$orig)` of the `r sum(s1$fixed)` gene sets significant in
`ssGSEA2.0-fixed` are also significant in `ssGSEA2.0-orig`, and pooled NES
correlations at `weight = 1` are high:

```{r luad-cor}
round(c(
  "orig vs. fixed" = nes_cor(luad$weight1$orig, luad$weight1$fixed),
  "orig vs. ssGSEA3.0" = nes_cor(luad$weight1$orig, luad$weight1$v3)
), 2)
```

The 28 curated HALLMARK gene sets shown in the original publication look
consistent across all three implementations (`*` marks FDR < 0.01):

```{r luad-heatmap, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 7.5}
compare_heatmaps(setNames(luad$weight1, method.names), luad$heatmap.terms$hallmark,
                 fdr.max = fdr.hallmark)
```

So the strongest signals found by `ssGSEA2.0-orig` are not artifacts of the
reordering, and previously published `weight = 1` results remain largely
reliable.

## Example 2: the same LUAD factors, REACTOME

HALLMARK's 50 gene sets are curated to be similar in size and narrow in scope.
REACTOME (1,167 gene sets after the `min.overlap = 10` filter, ranging from ten
to several hundred genes) is a harder test of the same data, scored at
FDR < 0.05:

```{r luad-reactome-score, eval = FALSE}
res.reactome <- ssGSEA3(
  input.ds = system.file("example", "LUAD_matrix_W_combined_signed_gc.gct", package = "ssGSEA3"),
  output.prefix = "luad_reactome",
  gene.set.databases = system.file("example", "reactome_subset.gmt", package = "ssGSEA3"),
  sample.norm.type = "rank", weight = 1, correl.type = "z.score",
  statistic = "area.under.RES", min.overlap = 10, nperm = 1000, seed = 42
)
```

This takes about 18 minutes on 10 cores (`ssGSEA2.0-orig`: about 9 minutes).

```{r luad-reactome-load}
reactome <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "luad_reactome_manuscript_results.rds",
                                package = "ssGSEA3"))
fdr.reactome <- 0.05

sig.reactome <- sapply(c("weight0", "weight1"), function(w) {
  sapply(reactome[[w]], function(r) sum(is_sig(r, fdr.reactome)))
})
dimnames(sig.reactome) <- list(method.names, c("weight = 0", "weight = 1"))
sig.reactome

round(c(
  "orig vs. fixed" = nes_cor(reactome$weight1$orig, reactome$weight1$fixed),
  "orig vs. ssGSEA3.0" = nes_cor(reactome$weight1$orig, reactome$weight1$v3)
), 2)
```

```{r luad-reactome-compare, include = FALSE}
r1 <- lapply(reactome$weight1, is_sig, fdr.max = fdr.reactome)
pct <- function(a, b) round(100 * (a - b) / b)
```

The pattern seen on HALLMARK is clearer here. Despite NES correlation of
`r round(nes_cor(reactome$weight1$orig, reactome$weight1$fixed), 2)`,
`ssGSEA2.0-fixed` finds `r -pct(sig.reactome[2, 2], sig.reactome[1, 2])`% fewer
significant gene sets than `ssGSEA2.0-orig` at `weight = 1`. Almost all of its
calls are shared with `ssGSEA2.0-orig` (`r sum(r1$fixed & r1$orig)` of
`r sum(r1$fixed)`), but it misses `r sum(r1$orig & !r1$fixed)`, and some of those
are relevant to LUAD, such as FGFR1 signaling and cellular senescence.
`ssGSEA3.0` finds `r sig.reactome[3, 2]`, a
`r pct(sig.reactome[3, 2], sig.reactome[2, 2])`% increase over `ssGSEA2.0-fixed`.
Fifteen representative gene sets significant in both `ssGSEA2.0-orig` and
`ssGSEA3.0` but missed by `ssGSEA2.0-fixed` at `weight = 1` (manuscript Figure 2D;
`*` marks FDR < 0.05):

```{r luad-reactome-heatmap-w1, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
compare_heatmaps(setNames(reactome$weight1, method.names),
                 reactome$heatmap.terms$reactome.fixed.missed, fdr.max = fdr.reactome,
                 labels = short_reactome)
```

At `weight = 0`, both `ssGSEA2.0` implementations find `r sig.reactome[1, 1]`
significant gene sets and `ssGSEA3.0` finds `r sig.reactome[3, 1]`
(`r pct(sig.reactome[3, 1], sig.reactome[1, 1])`% more), including PI3K signaling
and aberrant cell-cycle regulation. Fifteen representative gene sets significant
only in `ssGSEA3.0` at `weight = 0` (manuscript Figure 2E):

```{r luad-reactome-heatmap-w0, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
compare_heatmaps(setNames(reactome$weight0, method.names),
                 reactome$heatmap.terms$reactome.v3.only.w0, fdr.max = fdr.reactome,
                 labels = short_reactome)
```

So `ssGSEA3.0` fixes the calibration problem in `ssGSEA2.0-orig` without giving
up as much detection power as `ssGSEA2.0-fixed`, and the `weight = 0` result
suggests that feature-level bootstrapping itself has more power than gene-label
permutation.

## Example 3: PTM-SEA on a PI3K-inhibitor perturbation dataset

The second dataset (installed with the package in its `example/` folder) is site-centric phosphoproteomics
from the original PTM-SEA publication (Krug et al. 2019 -- see the package
`README` for the full citation): T47D breast cancer cells treated with the
PI3Kα inhibitor BYL719 vs. DMSO for 6h and 24h. The input values are log-signed
p-values from a moderated two-sample t-test at each timepoint. Because these
are not measured values, they are scored at `weight = 0` against PTMsigDB
v2.0.0's human flanking-sequence signatures:

```{r ptmsea-score, eval = FALSE}
res.ptmsea <- ssGSEA3(
  input.ds = system.file("example", "PI3K_pert_logP_n2x23936.gct", package = "ssGSEA3"),
  output.prefix = "pi3k",
  gene.set.databases = system.file("example", "ptm.sig.db.all.flanking.human.v2.0.0.gmt", package = "ssGSEA3"),
  sample.norm.type = "rank", weight = 0, correl.type = "rank",
  statistic = "area.under.RES", min.overlap = 5, nperm = 1000, seed = 42
)
```

This takes about 9 minutes on 10 cores (`ssGSEA2.0-orig`: about 4 minutes). At
`weight = 0` the two `ssGSEA2.0` implementations are equivalent, so as in the
manuscript only `ssGSEA2.0-fixed` is compared with `ssGSEA3.0`:

```{r ptmsea-load}
pi3k <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "pi3k_ptmsigdb_manuscript_results.rds",
                            package = "ssGSEA3"))
fdr.pi3k <- 0.05
p0 <- lapply(pi3k$weight0, is_sig, fdr.max = fdr.pi3k)

round(c(
  "NES Pearson r" = nes_cor(pi3k$weight0$fixed, pi3k$weight0$v3),
  "NES Spearman rho" = nes_cor(pi3k$weight0$fixed, pi3k$weight0$v3, method = "spearman")
), 2)

c("ssGSEA2.0-fixed" = sum(p0$fixed), "ssGSEA3.0" = sum(p0$v3),
  "both" = sum(p0$fixed & p0$v3), "ssGSEA3.0 only" = sum(p0$v3 & !p0$fixed))
```

`ssGSEA3.0` keeps most of `ssGSEA2.0-fixed`'s significant signatures
(`r sum(p0$fixed & p0$v3)` of `r sum(p0$fixed)`) while finding
`r pct(sum(p0$v3), sum(p0$fixed))`% more overall -- far more than the
`r pct(sig.reactome[3, 1], sig.reactome[1, 1])`% gain on REACTOME at `weight = 0`.
Many of the added signatures sit on the PI3K signaling axis this experiment
perturbs: upstream activators (PDK1, AMPKA2), downstream targets (p70S6K, SGK1),
MAPK-pathway crosstalk, and the cell-cycle response. Thirty-five representative
signatures significant in `ssGSEA3.0` but not `ssGSEA2.0-fixed` (manuscript
Figure 3C; `*` marks FDR < 0.05):

```{r ptmsea-heatmap, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 9}
compare_heatmaps(setNames(pi3k$weight0, method.names[c("fixed", "v3")]),
                 pi3k$heatmap.terms$pi3k.v3.only, fdr.max = fdr.pi3k)
```

The added calls cluster around the perturbed pathway rather than scattering
across unrelated biology, consistent with a genuine power advantage that is
most pronounced for directional gene sets.
